prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s dark in here, the dark inside of a man in the dark. It’s not night. One hears crows overhead, dawn fowl caws, the shod soles again treading their sunlit plots above. One grows dotish-fond of such things. Long live the things, their ways, their roots pushed goatish & gray through the skull, in this earth that gaily spins though one has crossed its smutted green threshold to reign in a crate. We have done no wrong, my friends, & yet we find ourselves soiled, sold, carbonized teeth in a moss-riven jaw. Once I sat on a stool as my grandmother told me of heaven. She cleaned fish for our living. I saw how her rusty black knife unseamed the sunset in each belly—coral, ochre, carmine, raw, lice-infested sunsets in a pail. So many nights. Night in the kitchen shack, night at the crumbling edge of our milk-pond province, a blade, lone cricket raving in the lawn.

Because your original text is deeply poetic, gothic, and literary (reminiscent of authors like Samuel Beckett or Cormac McCarthy), "polishing" it professionally means enhancing its lyrical cadence, vocabulary, and flow while preserving its evocative, haunting tone. 

Here are three options, ranging from a subtle literary refinement to a fully elevated prose style.

### Option 1: Refined & Lyrical (Recommended)
*This option maintains the original, fragmented rhythm and poetic voice while smoothing out sentence transitions.*

> "It is dark in here—the deep, internal darkness of a man entombed in shadow. Yet it is not night. Above, one hears crows overhead, the calls of dawn fowl, and shod soles once more treading their sunlit plots of earth. One grows foolishly fond of such things. Long live these details, their enduring ways, and their roots that push goatish and gray through the skull—here in this earth that gaily spins, though one has already crossed its smutted green threshold to reign within a crate. We have done no wrong, my friends, yet we find ourselves soiled, sold—like carbonized teeth set in a moss-riven jaw. 
> 
> Once, I sat upon a stool as my grandmother spoke to me of heaven. She cleaned fish for our living, and I watched as her rusty, blackened knife unseamed the sunset within each belly—yielding coral, ochre, and carmine, raw and lice-infested sunsets tumbling into a pail. So many nights passed like this: night in the kitchen shack, night at the crumbling edge of our milk-pond province, marked only by the flash of a blade and a lone cricket raving in the lawn."

---

### Option 2: Elegant & Fluid Narrative
*This option creates a smoother, more cinematic prose flow while keeping every single detail and image intact.*

> "It is dark here—the pitch darkness inside a man confined to the dark. Yet it is not night. One still hears the crows overhead, the caws of dawn fowl, and iron-shod soles again treading their sunlit plots above. One grows dotingly fond of such modest things. Long live those things, their ways, and their roots pushed goatish and gray through the skull, set within this earth that spins gaily on, even as one crosses its smutted green threshold to reign inside a crate. We have committed no wrong, my friends, yet here we lie: soiled, betrayed, like carbonized teeth in a moss-riven jaw. 
> 
> Once, I sat on a stool while my grandmother told me of heaven. She gutted fish for our living. I watched her rusty black knife unseam the sunset inside each belly—coral, ochre, and carmine, raw, lice-infested sunsets falling into a bucket. So many nights. Night in our kitchen shack, night at the crumbling edge of our milk-pond province—just a blade, and a lone cricket raving in the grass."

---

### Option 3: Modern Literary High-Style
*This option tightens the syntax for maximum emotional weight and poetic precision.*

> "It is dark here, the internal gloom of a man swallowed by shadow. It is not night. From above come the calls of crows, the caws of morning fowl, and the scrape of shod soles treading their sunlit plots once more. One becomes foolishly fond of such fragments. Long live these things, their quiet ways, their roots thrusting goatish and gray through the skull—all upon an earth that gaily spins, even as one crosses its smutted green threshold to reign inside a crate. We have done no wrong, my friends, yet we find ourselves soiled, bartered away, like carbonized teeth in a moss-riven jaw. 
> 
> Once, I sat upon a stool while my grandmother spoke to me of heaven. She cleaned fish to keep us alive. I saw how her rusty black knife unseamed a sunset in every belly—yielding coral, ochre, and carmine, raw, lice-ridden sunsets heaped in a pail. So many nights: night in the kitchen shack, night at the crumbling margin of our milk-pond province, illuminated only by a blade and the voice of a lone cricket raving in the lawn."

---

### Key Adjustments Made:
* **"Dotish-fond"** was refined to *"foolishly fond"* or *"dotingly fond"* for better cadence while preserving the meaning of affection born of sentimentality/decline.
* **Grammar & Flow:** Converted raw fragments (e.g., *"dawn fowl caws"*, *"a blade, lone cricket raving"*) into cohesive clauses that preserve the poetic rhythm without feeling ungrammatical.
* **Imagery Retention:** Kept all vivid descriptors intact (*carbonized teeth, moss-riven jaw, goatish & gray roots, milk-pond province, coral/ochre/carmine*).
outputs.L2:
A profound gloom fills this space, akin to the internal shadow of someone submerged in obscurity, though it is not actually nighttime. From up above, one can hear the morning calls of scavengers and roosters, alongside the heavy tread of shod feet moving across bright, sun-drenched ground. One develops an almost foolish affection for such ordinary noises. May these surface realities and their routines endure—their coarse, grayish tendrils driving directly through a person's brain as the cheerful globe keeps rotating, even after one has stepped past its dirty green border to occupy a mere wooden box. We are completely innocent, my companions, yet here we lie: degraded, traded away, reduced to blackened teeth set within a bone fractured by moss. 

I remember perching on a small seat while my grandmother spoke of paradise. She earned our sustenance by gutting fish. I watched her dark, corroded blade slice open their abdomens to spill out bucketfuls of visceral sunsets—shades of pink, yellow-brown, and deep red, raw and teeming with parasites. Endless evenings were spent like this in our humble cooking hut on the deteriorating outskirts of a dairy-pond region, defined by a single metal blade and an isolated cricket shrieking wildly from the grass.
outputs.L3:
The rough, splinted wood presses tightly against my shoulders, sealing me inside a dark, crate-like void where the air is thick and stale. Just inches above this wooden tomb, the sunlit world continues its careless rhythm. I can hear the muffled scraping of boots on cobblestones, the warm drone of distant conversation, and the occasional burst of laughter—a vibrant, glowing reality that continues without me, blissfully unaware of the cruel injustice taking place beneath its feet.

Yet, despite the grim reality of my confinement, I find no bitterness in listening to those sounds. Instead, a quiet, lingering fondness washes over me. The mundane echoes of everyday life—a creaking wagon wheel, the faint calling of a street vendor, the simple sigh of a stranger—become precious lifelines. In this cramped gloom, these distant signs of humanity are a gentle reminder of the world’s enduring beauty, even if I am barred from participating in it.

Beside me in the dark, the stifled breaths of my companions rustle against the wooden floorboards. We are decaying here together, abandoned to a quiet, rotting end by those who betrayed us. We committed no crime, harbored no malice, and did nothing to warrant such a sinister fate. We are innocent men doomed by treachery, left to wither in a dark corner of the world while our captors walk freely in the light. 

To escape the suffocating weight of this reality, my mind drifts backward in time. I vividly recall a scene from my childhood: my grandmother sitting on a worn wooden stool, her calloused hands slick with the iridescent, colorful scales of fresh fish. As her knife deftly prepped the day’s catch to ensure our family’s survival, her voice remained gentle, weaving soft tales of a radiant, painless heaven. Even as blood spilled across her apron, her words carried a quiet grace, teaching me that beauty and suffering often inhabit the exact same space.

Now, as the pitch-blackness of my current prison settles heavy upon my eyes, it no longer feels entirely foreign. This pervasive dark echoes the quiet, moonless nights of my impoverished hometown. Back then, when the lamps burned out and the village fell silent, the shadow was not a enemy, but a comfort. In this suffocating crate, surrounded by betrayal and decay, I hold fast to that memory—finding a strange, quiet peace in the darkness that once held me as a child.
outputs.L4:
The timber was so close it felt like an extension of my own bones. In the suffocating, pitch-black interior of the crate, breathing was a conscious effort, a slow pulling of dust-laden air into cramped lungs. My knees were wedged against my chest, my shoulders pressed hard against the unyielding oak. I had committed no crime—no thief’s night-work, no violence, no betrayal—yet I had been cast into this nameless obscurity, discarded like forgotten freight in a place forgotten by light. 

To surrender to the dark meant to allow the mind to rot, so I anchored myself to the thin seams where the wooden planks failed to flush completely. Through those microscopic slits came the only proof that a universe still existed beyond my wooden coffin. 

I learned to live through my ears. I listened to the muffled cadence of the sunlit world far above: the heavy, rhythm of boots dragging across dirt, the distant, laughter of a passing child, the quiet hum of flies swirling in the ambient warmth. I could feel the solar heat penetrating the top planks, a pale, phantom warmth that teased the top of my scalp. Up there, the world was bathed in brilliant, uncaring gold. Down here, I was a ghost awaiting a body.

When the silence grew too heavy and the shadows threatened to crush my ribcage, I retreated into the sanctuary of my youth. I did not summon grand events or profound conversations, but rather the sharp, visceral fragments of sensory truth that my body still remembered.

Most of all, I thought of my grandmother on the salt-stained porch of my childhood home. 

I could see her as clearly as if she were standing in the dark beside me: her skin cured by decades of coastal sun, her hands thick and scarred, yet holding a long-bladed knife with absolute, effortless grace. The summer heat back then had been thick enough to drink, buzzing with the scent of ozone, dry grass, and pine. On a low wooden bench before her lay the morning’s catch—stiff, silver-scaled fish brought up from the cool depths of the bay.

I remembered watching her press the tip of the steel into the vent of a fish, slicing upward in one smooth, practiced stroke. As the wet silver yielded, it opened to reveal an astonishing interior world: the raw, translucent bellies bathed in shades of bruised magenta, pale coral, and fiery sunset-orange. The contrast was always a shock—that beneath such dull, armor-like scales lay a hidden burst of brilliant, vibrant color, glistening and warm under the unforgiving sky. 

She would work in silence, her dark eyes focused, her hands painted in the wet, metallic sheen of the sea, stripping away the waste to expose what was pure and nourishing. 

Sitting in the cramped blackness of my prison, that memory became my salvation. The vividness of it—the cold flash of steel, the sharp tang of salt, the dazzling, sunset-hued flesh spilling out into the blinding light—filled the void around me. It was a sensory riot that the darkness could not extinguish.

They had stripped me of my freedom, my movement, and the sun itself. They had reduced my world to a box no larger than a chest of drawers. But as I closed my eyes and breathed in the memory of those sunset bellies, I knew they had failed to touch what mattered. A person’s humanity is not defined by the box they are forced into, but by the light they choose to carry inside it. In the quiet horror of my confinement, those bright, bloody memories were proof that I had lived, that I loved, and that—despite the darkness—I was still alive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, poetic monologue in the style of Cormac McCarthy or Samuel Beckett from the perspective of a man trapped underground in a wooden crate.
counterfactuals.output:
Six boards. Six pine boards and the cold, wet belly of the earth pressed down upon the lid. A box for a man. Or a man shaped for a box. No matter. The fit is close enough.

The dark in this place is not the absence of light. No. It is a thing made of grease and iron. It fills the mouth before you can shut it. It crawls into the ear like a beetle and nestles there, heavy and quiet. I breathe it in and it stays. A grey silt upon the lungs. 

In the beginning, I pushed. Ah. A fool’s errand. I threw my knees against the lid, and the oak creaked, and the dirt above gave a little shudder, a soft *sift-sift* through the cracks, falling into my eyes, into my open, screaming mouth. A rain of dry ash. The earth does not care for the man beneath it. It knows only its own weight. A thousand pounds of loam and root and dead beetles, holding me down like a hand.

So. We do not push anymore. We lie still. 

My left shoulder is wedged against a knot in the wood. A hard, weeping eye of sap. I can smell it—the old forest, blinding and green, cut down and sawed and nailed shut around my ribs. A strange thing, to be killed by a tree that died ten years ago. Was it a dry summer when they felled it? Did the birds fly out of its crown? They are flying now, somewhere. High up in the blue, where the wind blows cold and clean over the scrub-oak. They fly, and the sun strikes their wings, and down here I am sucking the last stale spit out of my own cheek.

Listen. 

Do you hear it? No. Nothing. Not even the worms. They have better places to be. The earth is vast and wet and full of softer meats than this.

My hands are pinned to my thighs. I can move the thumbs. *One, two. One, two.* A tiny dance for an audience of nails. Iron nails, bleeding red rust into the dark. If I had a knife, I would carve my name into the pine, but what is a name to a stone? God has forgotten the grammar of names anyway. He speaks in drought and lightning and the long, silence of the clay. He looks down at this patch of weeds and He sees only dirt, smooth and untroubled by the breath dying six feet below it.

The air is thin now. Small as a bird’s heart. I take a little, and it burns. I hold it, and my chest aches like an old hinge. 

How long? A day? Three? Time has no edges here. It is just a shape that shrinks. 

Try to turn the head. Go on. A quarter inch to the left. Ah. The cheek against the damp grain. There. That’s better. Or worse. No difference. 

The light is coming now. Not from the outside, no, there is no light up there, only the blind stars grinding against the night. The light is inside the skull. A little white fire behind the eyes, burning through the flesh, burning through the pine, spreading out into the dark dirt until the whole world is a hot, blinding spark, and then—

Nothing. 

Breath in. 

No. 

Breath out. 

Ah. There it goes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose piece starting from inside a grave or crate, looking back on a childhood memory of a grandmother cleaning fish while talking about heaven.
counterfactuals.output:
There is a pine splinter pressed against my left temple, and the smell of raw pitch is slowly losing its fight against the heavier, sweeter scent of damp loam. Space is short here. My knees are locked, my elbows pinned to my ribs by the narrow walls of the box. But the dark is not hostile; it is merely patient. It holds me the way the deep mud at the bottom of the pond holds the roots of the lilies, waiting for the ice to break.

Above me, a slow, rhythmic thudding tells me the earth is being shoveled back into place. *Thump. Slide. Thump.* 

The sound rubs against the lid of my crate, grit scraping on wood, and in the blackness, the friction turns into the sound of a blade. *Scritch. Scritch. Scritch.*

Suddenly, I am eight years old again, sitting on the sun-bleached steps of the back porch. The air smells of wet zinc, scales, and the sulfurous heat of an August afternoon. 

Grandma sits on an upturned milk crate before her wooden cleaning bench, her apron soaked through with pond water and fish blood. In her left hand, she holds a yellow perch, its belly pale and swollen, its fins spiky and stiff. In her right hand is her bone-handled paring knife, dull at the tip but sharp enough along the belly to shave the hair off an arm.

*Scritch.* 

She runs the back of the blade against the grain of the fish. A shower of tiny, mica-like scales flies up, sticking to her forearms, her chin, and the front of my bare knees. They glisten like sequins in the hard light.

"Is it hurtin' him?" I ask, flinching as a burst of silver lands on my cheek.

"He’s past hurting, child," she says without stopping. Her hands are gnarled, the knuckles swollen like oak galls, but they move with an terrifying, beautiful economy. "He’s out of the net now. All the thrashing is done."

She slices the belly open from vent to throat with a soft, wet pop. With a slick flick of her thumb, she scoops out the tangled, glistening innards—the purple liver, the translucent swim bladder, the dark thread of blood along the spine—and flips them into a rusted tin bucket where flies hum in frantic circles.

I lean back, nauseated and fascinated. "Where does he go now?"

"Into the skillet, mostly," she chuckles, her voice like gravel turning in a riverbed. Then she pauses, turning the fish under the thin stream of water running from the garden hose. The water washes away the smears of dark blood, leaving the flesh underneath pearlescent, translucent, and cold. 

She looks at me over the rims of her reading glasses, her eyes milky with cataracts but fierce with a quiet certainty. 

"People talk about heaven like it’s a city made of glass and gold," she says, her thumb smoothing down the clean, hollowed cavity of the fish. "Like you get wings and a nightgown. That’s just church-talk for people who are afraid of the dirt."

She lays the clean fish on a damp newspaper and reaches for a bullhead catfish, its dark, scaleless skin slick as oil.

"Heaven ain't a place you go to build a house," she tells the fish, or me, or the sun. "Heaven is just the scraping off. You spend sixty, seventy years swimming around in the mud at the bottom of the lake, growing thick armor so the rocks don't break you, swallowing hook after hook just trying to stay fed. You get heavy with it. You get scarred up and dark."

She makes a swift incision behind the catfish's gills and grabs its skin with a pair of rusty pliers, pulling it back in one smooth, tearing motion to reveal the pale, immaculate meat beneath.

"Dying is just God taking his knife to you," she says softly, rinsing the skinless fish until it glows like porcelain in the bucket of ice water. "He scrapes off the armor. He pulls out the dark stuff you’ve been carrying in your belly. He washes you clean until there ain't a scrap of dirt left on you, and then he drops you back into the deep water. Only this time, you don't drown, and you don't get caught."

*Thump. Slide.*

The memory dissolves back into the dark. The splinter still presses into my temple. The air in the crate is getting thick, heavy with my own quiet breathing, but the panic will not come. 

I lie still in the tight pine box, beneath the weight of the garden, feeling the cold seep slowly through the wood. I can feel the heavy armor I wore for so long—the old grudges, the tired bones, the thick, stubborn scales of my pride—beginning to loosen in the damp. 

The earth above me settles with a final, heavy sigh. It is dark, yes. But I am waiting for the blade. I am waiting for the water. I am waiting to be washed clean enough to swim.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a dense, visceral Southern Gothic passage about an innocent man buried alive. Focus on sensory imagery—crows overhead, dirt, fish guts resembling sunsets, and a feeling of quiet resignation. Use rich, archaic vocabulary and lyrical cadence.
counterfactuals.output:
The sky narrowed to a hemorrhaging seam between the rough pine planks, a bruised sliver of dusk that bled like the freshly spilled offal of river-catfish—all slick, violet iridescence and crimson gut-string, glistening with the terrible, rot-sweet majesty of a dying sun. High above the pit, where the humors of the low-country swamp hung thick as rendered lard, a synod of crows wheeled in jagged circles. Their harsh, rasping caws sheared through the humid air like rusty scythes through dead cane, a dark litany for a corpse still warm with breath. 

He lay prone in the shallow trench of alluvial clay, his soul entirely unblemished by the wickedness they had pinned upon his chest, yet his flesh yielded without struggle to the cold, unblinking mathematics of their malice. 

Then came the spade-fall. 

The first shove of soil struck his breastbone with a soft, wet calamity, rich with the stench of worm-churned loam, drowned cypress root, and the iron taste of ancient rain. It pooled like heavy mercury in the hollows of his collarbones, sifting into the folds of his coarse linen shirt. He did not thrash against the suffocating descent. A marrow-deep quietus settled over him—a velvet, terrifying resignation as profound as the swamp’s own stagnant silence. He simply closed his eyes against the rising dark, surrendering his lungs to the encroaching weight. 

Black dirt pressed past his lips, a heavy, chthonic Eucharist that sealed his tongue. The rasping calls of the corvids overhead thinned to a faint, rhythmic thrumming, drowned under shovel upon shovel of fuliginous earth, until even the ghost of the sunset was smothered, and he was swallowed whole by the sweet, dark belly of the southern ground.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short stream-of-consciousness piece about mortality, rotting, and the contrast between childhood purity and a dark present.
counterfactuals.output:
Drip, tap, rust in the pipes, rust in the back of the throat—tastes like a cold copper coin tucked under the tongue. How did my hands get so translucent? Papery, yellowed, like an old paperback left out in the rain, swollen and smelling of wet silt. There’s a bruise on my forearm that I don’t remember earning, a purple blossom blooming under the skin, fermenting, dark wine creeping through the meat of me. 

Everything goes soft at the edges eventually. The pear on the counter is sinking into its own bottom, a sweet, sickening liquor pooling on the formica, attracting small, frantic flies that don't know they're eating death.

It wasn't always wet like this. It wasn't always heavy. 

Remember six? Seven? The sun was a hard, white anvil beating down on the asphalt, making the tar bubble, and we pop-pop-popped it with dirty thumbs. Dirt under the fingernails then was just mud, just worms, innocent slimy threads tangled in clover. Dandelion milk sticky on the wrists. Scabbed knees that bled bright, hot crimson—so red! so alive!—and smelled like salt and summer. We swallowed water straight from the coiled green hose, metallic and ice-cold, running until our lungs felt like clean paper bags inflating, bursting with air. We were going to live forever because the afternoon was a million miles wide and the sun refused to set.

Now the shadows don't just fall, they pool. They leak out from under the baseboards.

I can feel the marrow settling. A slow, quiet compaction. The teeth feel loose in their sockets today—just a fraction, just a ghost of a wobble—root rot, timber rot, soul rot. What happened to the light that used to live behind my eyes? It burnt out, or maybe it got choked by all the dust motes hanging in this stale room. The air here tastes like breath that’s been breathed three times already. Used up. 

I was a child once, wasn't I? Crisp as an apple snapped in half. Purity isn't something you lose; it’s something that spoils. It sits out on the porch until the frost hits it, turns it to black slime, sinks it back into the loam. 

Tick, tick, the clock or the pulse in my temple, pushing thick, dark oil through a rusting machine. The little boy with the sun-bleached hair is buried under thirty years of dead skin cells, a mountain of sloughed-off dust, exhalations, forgotten laughter. I am walking my own corpse around the kitchen. I am holding a mug of cold tea and watching the mold form its quiet, perfect, velvety green ring. Beautiful, almost. The way we go bad. The way the soil begs for us to just lie down, give up the heat, and let the damp take over. Soft. So terribly, terribly soft.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary excerpt featuring these elements: being buried or confined in a box, hearing life go on above, claiming innocence ("done no wrong"), and a vivid memory of a rusty knife opening a fish belly in a kitchen shack.
counterfactuals.output:
The cedar was too narrow for my shoulders, forcing my arms tight against my ribs like the folded wings of a dead bird. Above my face, pine boards bowed under the crushing weight of wet loam, dropping fine ribbons of silt into my eyes every time the earth settled. 

And yet, the world above went on breathing, entirely unconcerned with my burial. 

Through the soil and the thick timber, the sounds arrived muffled, rendered thick and heavy like voices heard underwater. I heard the distinct, hollow *clack-clack* of Mrs. Gable’s iron-shod heels moving across the porch. I heard the distant, rhythmic scrape of a corn-broom sweeping dust into the yard, and a boy’s whistle, high and careless, cutting through the autumn air. A wagon groaned in the lane, its iron wheels grinding gravel. People were drinking tea; they were tying their boots; they were watching the light turn yellow in the tops of the sweetgums. 

I pounded my knuckles against the lid until the skin split, but the earth swallowed the sound whole. 

*I have done no wrong,* I thought, the words repeating in my mind like the dull, heavy stroke of a pendulum. *I have done no wrong.* I had taken no man’s gold, set fire to no man’s barn, harbored no malice. I was a vessel filled with nothing but my own innocence, yet they had nailed me into the dark and left me to drink my own stale breath.

As the air thinned, the dark began to pulse with a hot, vivid light, and my mind fled the box, retreating into the heat of a memory thirty years old. 

I was back in the kitchen shack at the end of the salt pier, where the air always smelled of woodsmoke, wet dog, and old fat. The whitewash was peeling in long, curled scales from the cedar studs. On the grease-slicked pine table lay a striped bass, its scales gleaming like polished pewter in the slanting afternoon sun. Old Silas held it down with a calloused thumb pressed hard into its eye socket. 

In his right hand was the skinning knife—its blade narrow, ground thin by years on the whetstone, orange rust flaking in heavy, dry scabs along the spine. He pressed the pitted, jagged point into the fish’s vent. There was a quiet, wet *snick*, the sound of skin giving way, and then Silas drew the rusty steel upward in a single, fluid drag toward the gills. 

The belly unzipped. A ribbon of pale, pearlescent flesh parted, spilling out a wet, glistening knot of dark viscera—purple liver, silver air-bladder, and the coil of grey guts—steaming softly on the cold wood.

In the smothering pitch of the coffin, I could smell that rust and iron salt as if the blade were resting against my own throat. I lay there in the dark, slit open by my own innocence, while above me, the living kept sweeping their dust.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
